{ "item": { "id": "c484e924-5ec5-4c95-81ad-c8c31b702a7f", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Handling errors & retries", "short_description": "How Godzilla retries failed events, when they're dead-lettered, and how to replay them.", "body": "

Handling errors & retries

Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

Automatic retries

Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-retry-config.json|language=json|code={ "retry_policy": { "max_attempts": 5, "backoff": "exponential", "initial_delay_ms": 1000 } }}}

Dead-lettering

An event that exhausts its retries is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped silently.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=danger|title=Dead-lettered events don't retry themselves|body_html=

Once in the dead-letter queue, an event stays there until you replay it or explicitly discard it — it will not retry again on its own.

}}

Replaying events

Use the Events endpoint's replay action to re-run a specific dead-lettered event once the underlying issue is fixed.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=replay.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/events/evt_8f2c1a90/replay \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY"}}

Watching for failures

Subscribe to pipeline.failed via Webhooks so you find out about dead-lettered events before a customer does. See also Monitoring & alerts.

{ "item": { "id": "dc9f1302-e173-4034-9581-d06efea7d090", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Scheduling & triggers", "short_description": "Run a pipeline on a cron schedule or trigger it directly from incoming events.", "body": "

Scheduling & triggers

A pipeline runs either on a schedule or in response to incoming events. This guide covers both.

Scheduled pipelines

Set a schedule (a cron expression) when creating or updating a pipeline via the Pipelines endpoint. Godzilla runs the pipeline once per schedule tick, processing whatever new data is available from the source since the last run.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=schedule.json|language=json|code={ "schedule": "0 */4 * * *" }}}

Event-triggered pipelines

Omit schedule and the pipeline instead runs continuously, processing events as its source connector emits them — the right choice for sources like Kafka or a Webhook connector where near-real-time matters.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Choosing between them|body_html=

Use a schedule for sources that batch naturally (a nightly file drop to S3). Use event-triggered for anything where minutes matter.

}}

Pausing and resuming

A paused pipeline skips scheduled ticks entirely and buffers nothing for event-triggered sources — resuming picks up new events going forward, not a backlog. To reprocess a time range instead, see the replay flow in Handling errors & retries.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/062cc815-2b65-45b1-b36c-6ea67dfd1a0c}}|prev_label=Handling errors & retries|next_href={{cms:item/522ba05b-8a21-43dd-82ac-ece908ce14b4}}|next_label=Monitoring & alerts}}", "version_token": "79959961-9dce-4f2e-b4ca-b957b12122d0", "created_at": "2026-08-20T14:12:47.158Z", "updated_at": "2026-08-20T15:07:12.086Z", "placement_id": "8ed279da-c9eb-46e0-bd2f-4f15df9f1c76", "folder_id": "c3e0ba4a-a491-4265-9848-556d298e6b6b", "file_name": "scheduling-and-triggers" } }

This guide walks through creating a pipeline end to end: a source connector, a destination connector, and the pipeline that ties them together.

{ "item": { "id": "4d0a186a-d358-47c0-bd8f-26778f2732fe", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Schemas", "short_description": "How event payload shapes are declared, validated, and evolved in Godzilla pipelines.", "body": "

Schemas

A schema is a declarative contract that defines the expected structure, data types, and required fields for an event payload moving through a pipeline. Schemas prevent malformed records from propagating downstream and ensure data integrity across source and destination connectors.

Declaring a schema

Godzilla schemas follow standard JSON Schema (Draft-07) specifications. You define schemas per event type or attach them directly to pipeline ingress and egress stages.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=order-created.schema.json|language=json|code={ "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#", "title": "OrderCreatedPayload", "type": "object", "properties": { "order_id": { "type": "string" }, "customer_id": { "type": "string" }, "amount_cents": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 0 }, "currency": { "type": "string", "enum": ["USD", "EUR", "GBP"] }, "status": { "type": "string" } }, "required": ["order_id", "amount_cents", "currency"], "additionalProperties": false }}}

Validation & enforcement modes

When a pipeline processes an event, Godzilla validates the payload against the registered schema. You can configure how validation failures are handled using one of three enforcement modes:

  • strict — Any event failing validation is immediately rejected and routed to the pipeline's dead-letter queue.
  • warn — The event continues through the pipeline, but a platform warning event is emitted for monitoring and alerting.
  • drop — Invalid events are silently discarded without halting pipeline execution or triggering retries.
{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Validation failure handling|body_html=

In strict mode, validation errors do not retry endlessly. Because payload schema mismatches are deterministic, failed events bypass transient retries and move straight to the dead-letter queue. See Handling errors & retries for details on inspecting and replaying dead-lettered events.

}}

Schema validation in the pipeline lifecycle

Validation can occur at three points in a pipeline run:

  1. Ingress validation — Verified immediately after a source connector emits an event, ensuring source data conforms to expectations.
  2. Post-transform validation — Verified after transform steps run to confirm reshaped payloads match target specifications.
  3. Egress validation — Checked before writing to a destination connector to guarantee downstream compatibility.

Schema evolution & compatibility

As business requirements change, schemas evolve. Godzilla supports backward and forward compatibility rules to prevent breaking active pipelines:

  • Additive changes — Adding optional fields is backward-compatible and does not require pipeline downtime.
  • Breaking changes — Removing fields or adding new required fields requires creating a new pipeline version or using a transform step to migrate payload shapes.

Glossary

Short definitions for every term used throughout these docs.

Pipeline
A named, versioned workflow that moves data from a source connector, through optional transforms, to a destination connector.
Connector
A pre-built integration to an external system — a source, a destination, or both.
Event
The atomic unit of data moving through a pipeline, or a platform lifecycle notification like pipeline.failed.
Schema
A declarative contract specifying the structure, types, and validation rules for event payloads.
Webhook
An outbound HTTP request Godzilla sends to a URL you control when a subscribed event occurs.
Dead-letter queue
Where an event goes after exhausting its retries, rather than being dropped. See Handling errors & retries.
Cursor pagination
The pagination style used by every v2 list endpoint. See Limits, quotas & errors.
Quota
Usage allowances assigned to a workspace based on its plan tier, covering request throughput and monthly event volume. See Quotas & billing.
Workspace
The top-level account boundary an API key is scoped to.

Troubleshooting / FAQ

Common problems, and where in the docs to go for the full explanation.

My pipeline isn't processing events

Check the source connector's health field via the Connectors endpoint. A down connector stalls every pipeline that reads from it. If it's healthy, confirm the pipeline itself is active and not paused — see Scheduling & triggers.

Events keep failing and landing in the dead-letter queue

Walk through Handling errors & retries — it covers both diagnosing the failure and replaying events once fixed.

I'm not receiving webhook deliveries

Verify your endpoint returns a 2xx status and that you're checking X-Godzilla-Signature correctly — a rejected signature looks identical to a dropped delivery from the outside. Full details in the Webhooks endpoint reference.

I'm getting 429s

You've hit the standard-tier limit described in Limits, quotas & errors. Back off using the Retry-After header, or review Quotas & billing to learn about plan tiers and how overages are handled.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Migrating from v1?|body_html=

A number of \"it worked yesterday\" reports trace back to v1's offset pagination or polling patterns carried over into v2 code. See the Migration guide.

}}

Still stuck?

Reach the team via Support / Contact.

{ "item": { "id": "a860f0ef-76cc-4e8c-8e39-93122557671c", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Backfill historical data", "short_description": "Techniques and configurations for loading historical data ranges through Godzilla pipelines.", "body": "

Backfill historical data

Backfilling lets you stream historical data from your storage or database into downstream targets — bootstrapping new destinations, backpopulating historical records, or replaying data after schema changes.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Before you begin|body_html=

Ensure your source connector supports range queries or timestamp filtering. See Connecting a data source for connector details.

}}

1. Define a time-bounded source connector

Configure your source connector with start and end timestamps (or watermarks) to define the historical boundary. This prevents the backfill job from processing live events prematurely.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=backfill-source.json|language=json|code={ "type": "postgres", "direction": "source", "config": { "connection_string": "postgres://user:secret@db.example.com:5432/production", "query": "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2025-01-01T00:00:00Z' AND created_at < '2026-01-01T00:00:00Z'", "timestamp_column": "created_at" } }}}

2. Set batch size and concurrency controls

Historical backfills often involve large data volumes. Adjust your pipeline's batch size and concurrency limit to avoid exhausting memory or triggering rate limits on your destination system.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-backfill.json|language=json|code={ "name": "orders-backfill-2025", "source_connector_id": "conn_pg_orders_backfill", "destination_connector_id": "conn_snowflake_dw", "settings": { "batch_size": 5000, "concurrency": 4, "max_retries": 5 } }}} {{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Destination throughput|body_html=

Monitor destination write latency while the backfill runs. If destination response times spike, reduce pipeline concurrency.

}}

3. Run and monitor the backfill

Start the pipeline using the Pipelines endpoint. You can inspect event throughput and error rates via Monitoring & alerts.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=run-backfill.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines/orders-backfill-2025/start \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY"}}

4. Transitioning to real-time streaming

Once the backfill reaches the cutoff timestamp, switch the pipeline configuration or activate your real-time streaming pipeline. Godzilla ensures idempotent writes when keys are configured, preventing duplicate entries during handoff.

Next steps

Learn how to handle failed records during backfills in Handling errors & retries, or query processed records using the Events endpoint.

{ "item": { "id": "ef8b84f2-786b-403a-a737-33aafc2e4e2c", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Events", "short_description": "What an event is in Godzilla: the atomic unit of data moving through a pipeline, plus the platform's own lifecycle events.", "body": "

Events

An event is the atomic unit of data that moves through a Pipeline. Every record a source connector emits, every row a transform produces, and every write a destination connector performs is an event.

Event shape

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=event.json|language=json|code={ "id": "evt_8f2c1a90", "type": "order.created", "occurred_at": "2026-08-18T09:12:44Z", "source": "connector_postgres_orders", "payload": { "order_id": "ord_4471", "amount_cents": 4899 } }}}

Payload schemas & validation

The payload property contains the user data carried by the event. You can declare contract definitions for event payload shapes using Schemas. Godzilla validates payloads at ingress, transform, and egress boundaries to ensure data matches expected types and required attributes.

User data events vs. platform events

Godzilla distinguishes two kinds of events:

  • User data events — the records your pipelines process, shaped however your source system produces them.
  • Platform events — lifecycle notifications Godzilla itself emits: pipeline.started, pipeline.completed, pipeline.failed, connector.error. These are what power Webhooks.
{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Ordering|body_html=

Events are delivered in-order per source partition, not globally. Two events from different source partitions may be processed out of order relative to each other.

}}

Retries and dead-lettering

An event that fails a transform or destination write is retried with exponential backoff. After the configured retry limit, it is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped. See Handling errors & retries for how to configure and drain a dead-letter queue.

Keep an eye on a running pipeline without babysitting it manually.

Connector health

Poll a connector's health field via the Connectors endpoint, or better, subscribe to connector.error so you're notified the moment it degrades.

Choosing a connector type

You haveUse

args.body:
Error handling & recovery

Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

Automatic retries

Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-retry-config.json|language=json|code={ "retry_policy": { "max_attempts": 5, "backoff": "exponential", "initial_delay_ms": 1000 } }}}

Dead-lettering

An event that exhausts its retries is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped silently.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=danger|title=Dead-lettered events don't retry themselves|body_html=

Once in the dead-letter queue, an event stays there until you replay it or explicitly discard it — it will not retry again on its own.

}}

Replaying events

Use the Events endpoint's replay action to re-run a specific dead-lettered event once the underlying issue is fixed.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=replay.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/events/evt_8f2c1a90/replay \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY"}}

Watching for failures

Subscribe to pipeline.failed via Webhooks so you find out about dead-lettered events before a customer does. See also Monitoring & alerts.

args.short_description: Reshape, filter, and enrich events as they pass through a pipeline.
args.body:
Transforming events in flight

Transforms are intermediate processing steps applied to events as they travel between a source connector and a destination in a pipeline. You can use transforms to reshape payload structures, filter out unwanted records, and enrich events with additional context.

1. Reshaping events

Use reshape transforms to rename fields, restructure nested objects, or strip sensitive and unneeded keys before writing to downstream storage.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=reshape-transform.json|language=json|code={ \"type\": \"reshape\", \"config\": { \"rename\": { \"customer_email\": \"email\", \"amt_cents\": \"amount_cents\" }, \"drop\": [\"internal_notes\", \"raw_ip\"] } }}}

2. Filtering events

Filtering lets you conditionally route or drop events based on payload criteria. Non-matching events are discarded immediately, saving destination throughput and storage.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=filter-transform.json|language=json|code={ \"type\": \"filter\", \"config\": { \"condition\": \"payload.status == 'completed' && payload.amount_cents > 0\" } }}} {{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Dropped events|body_html=

Filtered-out events do not trigger retries or dead-letter queue entries; they are treated as successfully skipped.

}}

3. Enriching events

Enrichment transforms add metadata, computed values, or static contextual fields to the event payload before delivery.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=enrich-transform.json|language=json|code={ \"type\": \"enrich\", \"config\": { \"add_fields\": { \"environment\": \"production\", \"processed_by\": \"godzilla-pipeline-v2\" } } }}}

Configuring transforms in a pipeline

Transforms are supplied as an ordered array on the pipeline definition. Godzilla executes each transform sequentially for every event.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-with-transforms.json|language=json|code={ \"name\": \"orders-with-transforms\", \"source_connector_id\": \"conn_pg_orders\", \"destination_connector_id\": \"conn_snowflake_dw\", \"transforms\": [ { \"type\": \"filter\", \"config\": { \"condition\": \"payload.amount_cents > 0\" } }, { \"type\": \"reshape\", \"config\": { \"drop\": [\"raw_ip\"] } }, { \"type\": \"enrich\", \"config\": { \"add_fields\": { \"region\": \"us-east\" } } } ] }}} {{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Order of execution matters|body_html=

Because transforms run sequentially, placing filter steps first avoids unnecessary processing on events that will ultimately be dropped.

}}

Next steps

Learn how Godzilla deals with transformation and destination write failures in Error handling & recovery, configure steps via the Transforms endpoint, or manage your pipelines directly using the Pipelines endpoint.

args.body:
Scheduling & triggers

A pipeline runs either on a schedule or in response to incoming events. This guide covers both.

Scheduled pipelines

Set a schedule (a cron expression) when creating or updating a pipeline via the Pipelines endpoint. Godzilla runs the pipeline once per schedule tick, processing whatever new data is available from the source since the last run.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=schedule.json|language=json|code={ \"schedule\": \"0 */4 * * *\" }}}

Event-triggered pipelines

Omit schedule and the pipeline instead runs continuously, processing events as its source connector emits them — the right choice for sources like Kafka or a Webhook connector where near-real-time matters.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Choosing between them|body_html=

Use a schedule for sources that batch naturally (a nightly file drop to S3). Use event-triggered for anything where minutes matter.

}}

Pausing and resuming

A paused pipeline skips scheduled ticks entirely and buffers nothing for event-triggered sources — resuming picks up new events going forward, not a backlog. To reprocess a time range instead, see the replay flow in Error handling & recovery.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/c484e924-5ec5-4c95-81ad-c8c31b702a7f}}|prev_label=Error handling & recovery|next_href={{cms:item/522ba05b-8a21-43dd-82ac-ece908ce14b4}}|next_label=Monitoring & alerts}}

Building your first pipeline

This guide walks through creating a pipeline end to end: a source connector, a destination connector, and the pipeline that ties them together.

args.body:
Schemas

A schema is a declarative contract that defines the expected structure, data types, and required fields for an event payload moving through a pipeline. Schemas prevent malformed records from propagating downstream and ensure data integrity across source and destination connectors.

Declaring a schema

Godzilla schemas follow standard JSON Schema (Draft-07) specifications. You define schemas per event type or attach them directly to pipeline ingress and egress stages.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=order-created.schema.json|language=json|code={ \"$schema\": \"http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#\", \"title\": \"OrderCreatedPayload\", \"type\": \"object\", \"properties\": { \"order_id\": { \"type\": \"string\" }, \"customer_id\": { \"type\": \"string\" }, \"amount_cents\": { \"type\": \"integer\", \"minimum\": 0 }, \"currency\": { \"type\": \"string\", \"enum\": [\"USD\", \"EUR\", \"GBP\"] }, \"status\": { \"type\": \"string\" } }, \"required\": [\"order_id\", \"amount_cents\", \"currency\"], \"additionalProperties\": false }}}

Validation & enforcement modes

When a pipeline processes an event, Godzilla validates the payload against the registered schema. You can configure how validation failures are handled using one of three enforcement modes:

  • strict — Any event failing validation is immediately rejected and routed to the pipeline's dead-letter queue.
  • warn — The event continues through the pipeline, but a platform warning event is emitted for monitoring and alerting.
  • drop — Invalid events are silently discarded without halting pipeline execution or triggering retries.
{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Validation failure handling|body_html=

In strict mode, validation errors do not retry endlessly. Because payload schema mismatches are deterministic, failed events bypass transient retries and move straight to the dead-letter queue. See Error handling & recovery for details on inspecting and replaying dead-lettered events.

}}

Schema validation in the pipeline lifecycle

Validation can occur at three points in a pipeline run:

  1. Ingress validation — Verified immediately after a source connector emits an event, ensuring source data conforms to expectations.
  2. Post-transform validation — Verified after transform steps run to confirm reshaped payloads match target specifications.
  3. Egress validation — Checked before writing to a destination connector to guarantee downstream compatibility.

Schema evolution & compatibility

As business requirements change, schemas evolve. Godzilla supports backward and forward compatibility rules to prevent breaking active pipelines:

  • Additive changes — Adding optional fields is backward-compatible and does not require pipeline downtime.
  • Breaking changes — Removing fields or adding new required fields requires creating a new pipeline version or using a transform step to migrate payload shapes.

See also

Learn more about working with events and payloads:

  • Events concept — Structure and lifecycle of events in Godzilla.
  • Transforming events in flight — Reshape, filter, and enrich event payloads.
  • Error handling & recovery — Dead-letter queues and retry mechanisms.

args.short_description: What an event is in Godzilla: the atomic unit of data moving through a pipeline, plus the platform's own lifecycle events.
args.body:
Events

An event is the atomic unit of data that moves through a Pipeline. Every record a source connector emits, every row a transform produces, and every write a destination connector performs is an event.

Event shape

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=event.json|language=json|code={ "id": "evt_8f2c1a90", "type": "order.created", "occurred_at": "2026-08-18T09:12:44Z", "source": "connector_postgres_orders", "payload": { "order_id": "ord_4471", "amount_cents": 4899 } }}}

Payload schemas & validation

The payload property contains the user data carried by the event. You can declare contract definitions for event payload shapes using Schemas. Godzilla validates payloads at ingress, transform, and egress boundaries to ensure data matches expected types and required attributes.

User data events vs. platform events

Godzilla distinguishes two kinds of events:

  • User data events — the records your pipelines process, shaped however your source system produces them.
  • Platform events — lifecycle notifications Godzilla itself emits: pipeline.started, pipeline.completed, pipeline.failed, connector.error. These are what power Webhooks.
{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Ordering|body_html=

Events are delivered in-order per source partition, not globally. Two events from different source partitions may be processed out of order relative to each other.

}}

Retries and dead-lettering

An event that fails a transform or destination write is retried with exponential backoff. After the configured retry limit, it is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped. See Error handling & recovery for how to configure and drain a dead-letter queue.

args.short_description: Definitions for Godzilla's core terms, each linking to its full explanation.
args.body:
Glossary

Short definitions for every term used throughout these docs.

Pipeline
A named, versioned workflow that moves data from a source connector, through optional transforms, to a destination connector.
Connector
A pre-built integration to an external system — a source, a destination, or both.
Event
The atomic unit of data moving through a pipeline, or a platform lifecycle notification like pipeline.failed.
Schema

Troubleshooting / FAQ

Common problems, and where in the docs to go for the full explanation.

My pipeline isn't processing events

Check the source connector's health field via the Connectors endpoint. A down connector stalls every pipeline that reads from it. If it's healthy, confirm the pipeline itself is active and not paused — see Scheduling & triggers.

Events keep failing and landing in the dead-letter queue

Walk through Error handling & recovery — it covers both diagnosing the failure and replaying events once fixed.

I'm not receiving webhook deliveries

Verify your endpoint returns a 2xx status and that you're checking X-Godzilla-Signature correctly — a rejected signature looks identical to a dropped delivery from the outside. Full details in the Webhooks endpoint reference.

I'm getting 429s

You've hit the standard-tier limit described in Limits, quotas & errors. Back off using the Retry-After header, or review Quotas & billing to learn about plan tiers and how overages are handled.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Migrating from v1?|body_html=

A number of \"it worked yesterday\" reports trace back to v1's offset pagination or polling patterns carried over into v2 code. See the Migration guide.

}}

Still stuck?

Reach the team via Support / Contact.

args.short_description: Techniques and configurations for loading historical data ranges through Godzilla pipelines.
args.body:
Backfill historical data

Backfilling lets you stream historical data from your storage or database into downstream targets — bootstrapping new destinations, backpopulating historical records, or replaying data after schema changes.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Before you begin|body_html=

Ensure your source connector supports range queries or timestamp filtering. See Connecting a data source for connector details.

}}

1. Define a time-bounded source connector

Configure your source connector with start and end timestamps (or watermarks) to define the historical boundary. This prevents the backfill job from processing live events prematurely.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=backfill-source.json|language=json|code={ \"type\": \"postgres\", \"direction\": \"source\", \"config\": { \"connection_string\": \"postgres://user:secret@db.example.com:5432/production\", \"query\": \"SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2025-01-01T00:00:00Z' AND created_at < '2026-01-01T00:00:00Z'\", \"timestamp_column\": \"created_at\" } }}}

2. Set batch size and concurrency controls

Historical backfills often involve large data volumes. Adjust your pipeline's batch size and concurrency limit to avoid exhausting memory or triggering rate limits on your destination system.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-backfill.json|language=json|code={ \"name\": \"orders-backfill-2025\", \"source_connector_id\": \"conn_pg_orders_backfill\", \"destination_connector_id\": \"conn_snowflake_dw\", \"settings\": { \"batch_size\": 5000, \"concurrency\": 4, \"max_retries\": 5 } }}} {{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Destination throughput|body_html=

Monitor destination write latency while the backfill runs. If destination response times spike, reduce pipeline concurrency.

}}

3. Run and monitor the backfill

Start the pipeline using the Pipelines endpoint. You can inspect event throughput and error rates via Monitoring & alerts.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=run-backfill.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines/orders-backfill-2025/start \\\n -H \"Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY\"}}

4. Transitioning to real-time streaming

Once the backfill reaches the cutoff timestamp, switch the pipeline configuration or activate your real-time streaming pipeline. Godzilla ensures idempotent writes when keys are configured, preventing duplicate entries during handoff.

Next steps

Learn how to handle failed records during backfills in Error handling & recovery, or query processed records using the Events endpoint.

args.body:
Fan-out to multiple destinations

In many architectures, a single incoming stream of events needs to reach several downstream systems simultaneously — for example, updating an analytical data warehouse, indexing in Elasticsearch for fast search, and notifying third-party services over webhooks.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Independent processing|body_html=

Godzilla processes each destination branch independently. A slow or failing destination will not block or degrade delivery to other healthy destinations.

}}

1. Create multiple destination connectors

First, define destination connectors for each service receiving the stream. See Connecting a data source for configuration details.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-destinations.sh|language=bash|code=# Snowflake destination\ncurl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \\\n -H \"Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY\" \\\n -d '{\"name\":\"snowflake-warehouse\",\"type\":\"snowflake\",\"direction\":\"destination\",\"config\":{\"account\":\"...\"}}'\n\n# Elasticsearch destination\ncurl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \\\n -H \"Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY\" \\\n -d '{\"name\":\"es-search-index\",\"type\":\"elasticsearch\",\"direction\":\"destination\",\"config\":{\"endpoint\":\"https://...\"}}'}}

2. Define the fan-out pipeline

Create a pipeline specifying multiple destination connectors. You can optionally apply branch-specific transforms to shape the payload for each destination's schema.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-fanout.json|language=json|code={ \"name\": \"orders-multidest-fanout\", \"source_connector_id\": \"conn_pg_orders\", \"destinations\": [ { \"connector_id\": \"conn_snowflake_warehouse\", \"transforms\": [ { \"type\": \"enrich\", \"config\": { \"add_fields\": { \"layer\": \"dw\" } } } ] }, { \"connector_id\": \"conn_es_search_index\", \"transforms\": [ { \"type\": \"reshape\", \"config\": { \"drop\": [\"raw_sql\", \"binary_blob\"] } } ] } ] }}}

3. Configure retry policies per destination

Different downstream engines have varying availability characteristics. Set distinct retry thresholds and dead-letter queues per branch to prevent temporary destination outages from polluting upstream buffers.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Dead-letter isolation|body_html=

Dead-lettered events are recorded with the destination ID attached, allowing targeted replaying without duplicating events to already successful destinations.

}}

Next steps

Learn more about replay workflows in Error handling & recovery, or see how to trigger fan-out pipelines on schedules in Scheduling & triggers.
